statement: For an n x n real or complex matrix X, the matrix exponential e^X (also written exp X or exp(X)) is the n x n matrix given by the power series e^X = sum_{k=0}^{inf} X^k / k! = I + X + X^2/2! + X^3/3! + ... . It is the matrix counterpart of the ordinary exponential function and is used to solve systems of linear differential equations. Notation: these sheets reserve P, R and Q for state-estimation covariances, so the source's other uses of those letters are renamed here. The source's projection matrix P is written Pi, its rotation matrix R(theta) is written Rot(theta), its polynomials P(z) and Q_t(z) are written p(z) and q_t(z), and its Jordan similarity matrix P is written S. (Note on grounding: the supplied excerpt cuts off the defining series right after 'given by the power series'. The series form sum_{k=0}^{inf} X^k/k! is still shown explicitly in the source's projection-case expansion, and the nilpotent case refers back to 'the series expansion'.)

symbols.meaning: identity matrix (the k = 0 term of the series)
summation index of the power series
a diagonalizable matrix (in the Jordan–Chevalley split X = A + N), or a general matrix in e^{tA}
diagonal matrix of eigenvalues in A = U D U^{-1}
invertible matrix whose columns diagonalize A
nilpotent matrix, N^q = 0 for some integer q
Jordan form of X, X = S J S^{-1}
similarity matrix taking X to its Jordan form (the source writes P)
Jordan block of size a with eigenvalue lambda, equal to lambda I + N
projection (idempotent) matrix, Pi^2 = Pi (the source writes P)
rotation generator, G = b a^T - a b^T, for perpendicular unit vectors a and b
rotation matrix e^{G theta} (the source writes R(theta))
scalar polynomials with p(A) = 0, used in the Cayley–Hamilton / Laurent-series evaluation (the source writes P, Q_t)

properties.property: Diagonal matrix: if A = diag(a_1, ..., a_n), then e^A = diag(e^{a_1}, ..., e^{a_n}).
properties.why: sums and products of diagonal matrices act entry by entry, so the series also acts entry by entry on the diagonal

properties.property: Diagonalizable matrix: if A = U D U^{-1} with D diagonal, then e^A = U e^D U^{-1}. Worked example: A = [[1,4],[1,1]] = U diag(-1,3) U^{-1} with U = [[-2,2],[1,1]], so e^A = U diag(1/e, e^3) U^{-1} = [[(e^4+1)/(2e), (e^4-1)/e], [(e^4-1)/(4e), (e^4+1)/(2e)]].
properties.why: this reduces the problem to exponentiating a diagonal matrix

properties.property: Nilpotent matrix: if N^q = 0, then e^N = I + N + N^2/2 + N^3/6 + ... + N^{q-1}/(q-1)!, which is a matrix polynomial.
properties.why: every term with power q or higher is zero, so the series stops after finitely many terms

properties.property: Commuting sum: if X = A + N with A diagonalizable, N nilpotent and AN = NA (Jordan–Chevalley decomposition), then e^X = e^{A+N} = e^A e^N.
properties.why: the source states that the factorisation needs A and N to commute

properties.property: Similarity and Jordan form: if X = S J S^{-1}, then e^X = S e^J S^{-1}. For J = J_{a_1}(lambda_1) ⊕ ... ⊕ J_{a_n}(lambda_n), e^J = e^{lambda_1} e^{N_{a_1}} ⊕ ... ⊕ e^{lambda_n} e^{N_{a_n}}, because each block is J_a(lambda) = lambda I + N, so e^{J_a(lambda)} = e^lambda e^N.
properties.why: the exponential acts block by block on a direct sum, and lambda I commutes with N

properties.property: Projection: if Pi^2 = Pi, then e^Pi = sum_{k>=0} Pi^k/k! = I + (sum_{k>=1} 1/k!) Pi = I + (e - 1) Pi.
properties.why: every power Pi^k with k >= 1 equals Pi, so Pi factors out of the series

properties.property: Rotation: for G = b a^T - a b^T with a and b perpendicular unit vectors, define Pi = -G^2 = a a^T + b b^T. Then Rot(theta) = e^{G theta} = I + G sin(theta) + G^2 (1 - cos(theta)) = I - Pi + Pi cos(theta) + G sin(theta). In 2D, with G = [[0,-1],[1,0]], this is [[cos theta, -sin theta],[sin theta, cos theta]].
properties.why: powers of G reduce to plus or minus G and G^2, and the coefficients collect into the sine and cosine series; only the component in the ab-plane is rotated

properties.property: Polynomial form: by the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, e^{tA} can be written as a polynomial in A of degree n-1. If p(A) = 0 and (e^{tz} - q_t(z))/p(z) is entire, then e^{tA} = q_t(A).
properties.why: this gives a closed form that avoids summing the infinite series

properties.property: Numerical evaluation: computing e^X reliably and accurately is hard and still an active research topic. Matlab, GNU Octave, R and SciPy all use the Padé approximant.
properties.why: the hand methods above work for small matrices but are not what libraries use

assumptions.breaks_when: X is non-square, so X^k is undefined and so is the series.

assumptions.assumption: e^{A+N} = e^A e^N is used only when A and N commute.
assumptions.breaks_when: AN ≠ NA. The source says commutativity is needed for this step, so the split is not valid for general A and N.

assumptions.assumption: The diagonal shortcut e^A = U e^D U^{-1} needs A to be diagonalizable.
assumptions.breaks_when: A is not diagonalizable. Use the Jordan–Chevalley or Jordan-form route instead.

assumptions.assumption: The Jordan-form method needs an algebraically closed field (complex entries).
assumptions.breaks_when: you work over the reals with a matrix whose eigenvalues are complex: its Jordan form does not exist over the reals.

assumptions.assumption: The series stops after finitely many terms only for nilpotent matrices.
assumptions.breaks_when: N^q ≠ 0 for every q. The series is then infinite and the finite-polynomial formula does not apply.

failure_modes.mode: Exponentiating a sum as a product of exponentials
failure_modes.signature: e^{A+B} computed as e^A e^B gives a result that disagrees with the series
failure_modes.cause: A and B do not commute; the source states that commutativity is required for e^{A+N} = e^A e^N.

failure_modes.mode: Exponentiating entries instead of the matrix
failure_modes.signature: e^X computed entry by entry for a non-diagonal X
failure_modes.cause: entry-wise exponentiation equals the matrix exponential only for diagonal matrices, where sums and products act entry by entry.

failure_modes.signature: the eigenvector matrix U is not invertible, so U e^D U^{-1} cannot be formed
failure_modes.cause: X has a nontrivial Jordan block; its nilpotent part has to be handled through e^N.

failure_modes.signature: inaccurate or unreliable values from hand-rolled numerical methods
failure_modes.cause: computing the matrix exponential accurately is hard; standard libraries use the Padé approximant instead.

instantiation.why_here: Nothing in agrios_ws computes a matrix exponential itself. The only link is that ekf_local and ekf_global run robot_localization's EKF, and the algorithm behind that component depends on this result. No library source was shown, so nothing here says whether or where robot_localization forms e^X or e^{tA}.
instantiation.thin: names no parameter and maps none of the 17 symbols the sheet defines
